title: Three Prescriptions for Thinking More Clearly about Teaching, Part 3: Write More https://davestuartjr.com/three-prescriptions-for-thinking-more-clearly-about-teaching-part-3-write-more/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: The closing part of Dave Stuart Jr.'s series on clearer thinking adds the third prescription: balance consumption with creation by writing. He argues that thinking alone leaves ideas vague and conversation leaves them as rough drafts, whereas writing forces a person to order, connect, define and slow down. He offers three practical starting points for teachers: begin a blog, keep a journal, or write a memo or proposal on a real problem facing the school. Drawing on his own old notebooks and a current memo on the transition to high school, he describes writing as humbling because it exposes what he does not yet know. He justifies the time cost by calling reading and writing the most critical things he does professionally, since clearer thinking lets him skip or satisfice the unimportant and invest in what matters most.
points: Writing converts vague thoughts into concrete, ordered ones in a way that private thinking and even discussion do not.
Three low-barrier ways to start are a blog, a journal, or a memo on a live school problem, with consistency valued over ambition.
Writing a proposal for a real school issue is useful because it drives research and revision while revealing the limits of one's own understanding.
Reading and writing are framed as core professional work, not extras, because the clarity they create improves prioritization across a teacher's whole job.
quotes: Clear thinking yields better teaching and better living and wiser choices. We want to be clear thinkers. But it doesn't come automatically.
Few things clarify thinking the way that writing does. When I think something about teaching, it's a vague and nebulous thing in my mind.
But when I sit down to write the thing, then I'm forced to turn the abstract into the concrete. I have to order things. I'm forced to transition and connect and define and explain.
You don't need to have any grand aspirations for your blog — just the goal of consistent writing. Jeff's tips (second half of the post) are especially wise.

There's a box of spiral notebooks I scrawled in during my first few years as a teacher. I've been going back through them recently, and I'm amazed at how instrumental the act of writing was on my development as a thinker.
It's pushing me to read, research, and revise. It's forcing me to think more clearly. It's humbling me with what I don't know and how far I have to go before I'm an apt explainer.
And my answer is that writing and reading are the single most critical things that I do as a professional. Why? Because they make me a clearer thinker.
